name: Kagulu
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Petzell, Malin. 2008. The Kagulu language of Tanzania: grammar, texts and vocabulary. Cologne: Koeppe (Glottolog MED grammar; not open-access)

new_statements.quote: THE ACCENT. The accent is almost invariable on the penultimate, or last syllable but one. When otherwise, the accent is marked over its syllable, as in mehékulu, a married woman. When suffixes are added to a word, the accent is generally shifted so as to be on the last syllable but one.
new_statements.citation: Last, J. T. 1886. Grammar of the Kagúru language, Eastern Equatorial Africa. London: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge.
new_statements.locator: p. 3, Part I 'The Alphabet', subsection 'The Accent'
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Google Books page image of Last 1886, p. 3, running head 'THE ALPHABET.') and read it visually, not just the scanned. Under the heading 'THE ACCENT.' the page reads exactly: 'The accent is almost invariable on the penultimate, or last syllable but one. When otherwise, the accent is marked over its syllable, as in mehékulu, a married woman. When suffixes are added to a word, the accent is generally shifted so as to be on the last syllable but one.' — verbatim as quoted (the scanned file garbles only the heading, 'Tue ACCENT'). The surrounding material (alphabet with example words p. 2-3, Swahili~Kaguru l/r correspondences) is consistent; the saved search-within-volume snippets  indep…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; it is recomputed over suffixed forms (shifts rightward to stay penultimate). A few lexical exceptions carry non-penultimate accent, which Last marks with an acute (e.g. mehékulu, antepenultimate).
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost invariable' — occasional words with accent elsewhere, marked with an acute in Last's spelling (mehékulu 'a married woman'; demonstratives with final-vowel stress for distal emphasis, p. 44 snippet: '...stress is on the final vowel, so much the more is the distance denoted'). NB the modern grammar (Petzell 2008: 40-41), seen only second-hand via Kraska-Szlenk's 2008 review, apparently hedges: 'there is probably phrasal tone and not lexical tone' and gives examples of 'pre-antepenult' stress, which the reviewer suggests may be initial stress; Hyman 2013 lists Kagulu among Bantu languages with penultimate lengthening. Petzell 2015: 50 states Kagulu has no lexical or grammatical tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in citation forms as transcribed by a CMS missionary (1880s, Mamboya, U-Sagara); accent shifts with suffixation, i.e. computed over the full inflected word. Glottolog/Beidelman 1967 warn the grammar has Gogo material mixed in and many misprints; Marten 2010 calls it 'generally unreliable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Last 1886 describes 'Kagúru' as spoken in U-Sagara around the CMS Mamboya mission (the Kaguru 'sub-tribe' of the Sagara, called Mégi by the Maasai) = Kagulu kagu1239 (autonyms Chikagulu/Chimegi per Petzell 2015). Glottolog's note on this grammar: 'marred with numerous press errors' (Johnston 1922: 791) and 'much Gogo material mixed in it' (Beidelman 1967: 81). Petzell's data (2002-2006) are from Kilosa district (Mamboya/Berega/Gairo), same variety.

sources.citation: Kraska-Szlenk, Iwona. 2008. Review of M. Petzell, The Kagulu Language of Tanzania (Köppe 2008). Studies of the Department of African Languages and Cultures 42: 94-97.
sources.note: Second-hand report of Petzell 2008 ch. 2 (pp. 35-46): 'A presumably complex prosodic pattern of Kagulu is only signalled (pp. 40f.), with rather vague statements as to tone (e.g. "there is probably phrasal tone and not lexical tone", p. 41) and not very convincing claims about stress (the examples of rather unusual "pre-antepenult" stress on p. 41 could be perhaps cases of the initial stress).' (review p. 95)
